a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

b.   Explain how deletion is performed in a Binary Search Tree (BST).

Solution:
Explain how deletion is performed in a Binary Search Tree (BST)- 5
marks
CO-3;   The delete function deletes a node from the binary search tree.
SO-1,2;   However, utmost care should be taken that the properties of the binary   [10]
BL-3   search tree are not violated and nodes are not lost in the process.
Case 1: Deleting a Node that has No Children
we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
********** 5 **********
--- page 6 ---
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.

What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

SO-1,2 ;   1. Most Suitable Data Structure: Hash Table
BL-4   Justification:
• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.
•   It provides average-case O(1) time complexity for search,
insertion, and deletion.
• This makes it ideal for systems that require quick passenger
verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.
• Other structures like arrays, lists, or trees would result in O(n) or
O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

• A priority queue automatically arranges elements based on their
priority.

priority job with minimum running time be accessed.
a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

SO-1,2 ;   1. Most Suitable Data Structure: Hash Table
BL-4   Justification:
• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.
•   It provides average-case O(1) time complexity for search,
insertion, and deletion.
• This makes it ideal for systems that require quick passenger
verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.
• Other structures like arrays, lists, or trees would result in O(n) or
O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

• A priority queue automatically arranges elements based on their
priority.

priority job with minimum running time be accessed.
a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end

Free temp

A Define data structure and list its applications
A data structure is a specialized format for organizing, processing, and storing data in a computer system. It provides
a way to manage large amounts of data efficiently for various uses, such as searching, sorting, and updating
information. [2 Marks]
Applications: To write optimize computer programming solutions of real-life problems.

C Tree is not a Graph justify this statement with example.
A graph data structure is a collection of nodes (also called vertices) and edges that connect them. Nodes can
represent entities, such as people, places, or things, while edges represent relationships between those
entities. Graphs are used to model a wide variety of real-world systems, such as social networks, transportation
networks, and computer networks.
A tree data structure is a hierarchical data structure that consists of nodes connected by edges. Each node can
have multiple child nodes, but only one parent node. The topmost node in the tree is called the root node.
Trees are often used to represent hierarchical data, such as file systems, XML documents, and organizational
charts.
Key Differences Between Graph and Tree
Cycles: Graphs can contain cycles, while trees cannot.
Connectivity: Graphs can be disconnected (i.e., have multiple components), while trees are always connected.
Hierarchy: Trees have a hierarchical structure, with one vertex designated as the root. Graphs do not have this
hierarchical structure.

B What is Big O notation? Calculate the time complexity of linear search algorithm.
Big O notation is a mathematical notation used to describe the time complexity or space complexity of algorithms.
It provides a standardized way to compare the efficiency of different algorithms in terms of their worst-case
performance. Understanding Big O notation is essential for analysing and designing efficient algorithms.
Key Principles of Big O Notation: Big O notation expresses the upper bound of an algorithm’s time complexity,
analysing the worst-case scenario. It is denoted as O(f(n)), where f(n) represents the number of operations an
algorithm performs to solve a problem of size n.
Importance of Big O Notation: Big O notation helps in analysing the efficiency of algorithms by providing a way to
describe how the runtime or space requirements grow as the input size increases. It allows programmers to
compare different algorithms and choose the most efficient one for a specific problem. [ 2 Marks]

A Stack is suitable data structure to reverse the string” write a program in C/C++ to demonstrate it.
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#define MAX_SIZE 100
// Global stack and top variable declaration
char stack[MAX_SIZE];
int top = -1;
// Function to push a character onto the stack
void push(char data) {
if (top == MAX_SIZE - 1) {
printf("Stack Overflow!\n");
return;
}
top++;
stack[top] = data;
}
// Function to pop a character from the stack
char pop() {
if (top == -1) {
printf("Stack Underflow!\n");
return '\0';
}
char data = stack[top];
top--;
return data;
}
// Function to reverse a string using a stack
void reverse_string(char *str) {
int len = strlen(str);
// Push each character of the string onto the stack
for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
push(str[i]);
}
// Pop characters from the stack to reverse the string
for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
str[i] = pop();
}
}
int main() {
char text[MAX_SIZE];
printf("Input a string: ");
fgets(text, MAX_SIZE, stdin);
// Remove newline character from input
text[strcspn(text, "\n")] = '\0';
// Reverse the input string using the stack
reverse_string(text);
// Print the reversed string

A Explain the Greedy algorithm with example.
What Is a Greedy Algorithm? [6 Marks]
A Greedy algorithm is a problem-solving approach that makes the best possible choice at each step, hoping
that these local choices lead to a globally optimal solution.
•   It does not reconsider decisions once made.
•   Works well for problems where local optimum leads to global optimum.
•   Often faster and simpler than other approaches like dynamic programming.
•   May not always give the best solution for every problem.
Example: Fractional Knapsack Problem [ 4 Marks]
Problem: You have a knapsack with a weight limit. You want to fill it with items to maximize value. You can
take fractions of items.
Greedy Strategy: Choose items based on highest value-to-weight ratio.
Steps:
1.   Calculate value/weight for each item.
2.   Sort items by this ratio in descending order.
3.   Pick as much of the highest-ratio item as possible.
4.   Repeat until the knapsack is full.
B Compare Backtracking algorithm with Trial-and-Error approach.
What Is Backtracking? [5 Marks]
Backtracking is a systematic algorithmic technique for solving problems incrementally. It builds
candidates for the solution and abandons a candidate ("backtracks") as soon as it determines that the
candidate cannot possibly lead to a valid solution.
• Used in: puzzles (like Sudoku), constraint satisfaction problems (like N-Queens),
combinatorics, and decision trees.
• Key feature: It prunes the search space by abandoning paths that are clearly invalid.
What Is Trial-and-Error? [ 5 Marks]
Trial-and-Error is a more informal, brute-force method of problem-solving. It involves trying various
possibilities until one works, without necessarily following a structured or optimized path.
• Used in: everyday problem-solving, exploratory learning, and when no clear algorithm is
known.
• Key feature: It lacks a systematic way to avoid repeating failed attempts.

#include <stdio.h>

// Node structure
struct Node {
int data;

};
// Queue structure
struct Queue {
struct Node *front, *rear;
};
// Function to create a new node
struct Node* newNode(int data) {
struct Node* temp = (struct Node*)malloc(sizeof(struct Node));
temp->data = data;
temp->next = NULL;
return temp;
}
// Function to create an empty queue
struct Queue* createQueue() {
struct Queue* q = (struct Queue*)malloc(sizeof(struct Queue));
q->front = q->rear = NULL;
return q;
}
// Enqueue operation
void enqueue(struct Queue* q, int value) {
struct Node* temp = newNode(value);
if (q->rear == NULL) {
q->front = q->rear = temp;
return;
}
q->rear->next = temp;
q->rear = temp;
}
// Dequeue operation
void dequeue(struct Queue* q) {
if (q->front == NULL) {
printf("Queue is empty!\n");
return;
}
struct Node* temp = q->front;
q->front = q->front->next;
// If front becomes NULL, then change rear also
if (q->front == NULL)
q->rear = NULL;
printf("Dequeued: %d\n", temp->data);
free(temp);

Step-by-Step BFS Traversal (Starting from Node A)
Initialization:
•   Visited: []
• Queue: [A]
Step 1: Visit A
• Dequeue A
• Mark A as visited → Visited = [A]
• Enqueue neighbors of A: B, C → Queue = [B, C]
Step 2: Visit B
• Dequeue B
• Mark B as visited → Visited = [A, B]
• Enqueue unvisited neighbors of B: D, E → Queue = [C, D, E]
Step 3: Visit C
• Dequeue C
• Mark C as visited → Visited = [A, B, C]
• Enqueue unvisited neighbor of C: F → Queue = [D, E, F]
Step 4: Visit D
• Dequeue D
• Mark D as visited → Visited = [A, B, C, D]
• D has no unvisited neighbors → Queue = [E, F]
Step 5: Visit E
• Dequeue E
• Mark E as visited → Visited = [A, B, C, D, E]
• E has no unvisited neighbors → Queue = [F]

• Dequeue F
• Mark F as visited → Visited = [A, B, C, D, E, F]
•   F has no unvisited neighbors → Queue = []
Final BFS Traversal Order:
A → B → C → D → E → F

A Why greedy approach is better option for finding the shortest path? Compare it with genetic algorithm
[2+3 Marks]
Greedy algorithms like Dijkstra’s is widely used for shortest path problems in graphs with non-negative
weights.
Advantages:
•   Fast and efficient: Dijkstra’s algorithm runs in (O(V + E \log V)) time with a priority queue.
•   Deterministic: Always gives the same result for the same input.
• Optimal for specific cases: Guaranteed to find the shortest path in graphs with positive weights.
• Simple to implement: Uses queues and basic graph traversal.
•
How It Works:
• Always picks the node with the lowest cost from the source.
• Expands outward, updating shortest distances.
•   Stops when the destination is reached.
Genetic algorithms (GAs) are metaheuristic search techniques inspired by natural selection. They’re used
when the search space is huge or poorly understood.
Advantages:
•   Flexible: Can handle complex constraints and dynamic environments.
•   Global search: Explores multiple paths simultaneously.
•   Useful for NP-hard problems: Like traveling salesman or routing with constraints.
•
Limitations:
• No guarantee of optimality: May find a good solution, not necessarily the best.
•   Slower: Requires many generations and tuning of parameters.
•   Stochastic: Results vary between runs.
********** 10 **********
--- page 11 ---
Feature   Greedy Algorithm (e.g., Dijkstra)   Genetic Algorithm
Optimality   Guaranteed (for positive weights) Not guaranteed
Speed   Fast and efficient   Slower, depends on population size
Determinism   Deterministic   Stochastic
Complexity Handling Limited to well-defined graphs   Handles complex, dynamic constraints
Use Case   Routing, maps, networks   TSP, logistics, multi-objective problems
Implementation   Simple   Requires tuning (mutation, crossover, etc.)
• Use greedy algorithms when the problem is well-defined and optimality matters.
• Use genetic algorithms when the problem is complex, dynamic, or lacks a clear structure.
B Explain the expression tree with example [2+3 Marks]
An expression tree is a binary tree used to represent arithmetic expressions. Each leaf node is an operand
(like a number or variable), and each internal node is an operator (like +, −, ×, ÷).
Structure of an Expression Tree
• Operands (numbers/variables) → Leaf nodes
•   Operators (+, −, ×, ÷) → Internal nodes
•   Evaluation → Recursively evaluate left and right subtrees, then apply the operator
Example: Expression ((3 + 5) * (2 − 1))
Expression Tree:
*
/ \
+ -
/ \ / \
3 5 2 1
Evaluation Steps:
1. Evaluate left subtree: 3 + 5 = 8
2. Evaluate right subtree: 2 − 1 = 1
3. Apply root operator: 8 * 1 = 8
Traversals
Traversal Type   Result   Meaning
Inorder   3 + 5 * 2 − 1 Original expression (with parentheses for clarity)
Preorder   * + 3 5 − 2 1 Prefix notation
Postorder   3 5 + 2 1 − * Postfix notation
Applications

C What is AVL Tree? Demonstrate all of its rotations with example. [2+3 Marks]
An AVL Tree is a type of self-balancing Binary Search Tree (BST) where the difference in heights of the left and
right subtrees (called the balance factor) of any node is at most 1.
What Makes AVL Trees Special?
•   Balance Factor = Height of Left Subtree − Height of Right Subtree
•   For every node: Balance Factor ∈ {−1, 0, 1}
•   If the balance factor goes outside this range after insertion or deletion, the tree rebalances itself using
rotations.
Types of Rotations in AVL Trees
There are four types of rotations used to restore balance:
Case Rotation Type   Trigger Condition
1⃣   Left-Left (LL)   Insertion in left subtree of left child
2⃣   Right-Right (RR) Insertion in right subtree of right child
3⃣   Left-Right (LR) Insertion in right subtree of left child
4️⃣   Right-Left (RL) Insertion in left subtree of right child

D Compare the linear search with binary search approach and calculate its time complexity
********** 13 **********

It looks like you meant to compare linear search with another search approach—possibly binary search? Since
your message says "compare the linear search with linear search," I’ll assume you meant to compare linear
search vs binary search. Let’s dive into that, and I’ll also explain the time complexity of linear search.
Linear search (also called sequential search) checks each element in a list one by one until it finds the target
or reaches the end.
Characteristics:
• Works on unsorted or sorted data
• Simple to implement
• No preprocessing needed
Time Complexity:
Case   Time Complexity
Best Case   O(1) (target is first element)
Average Case O(n)
Worst Case O(n) (target is last or not present)
Binary search is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that works only on sorted arrays. It repeatedly divides the
search interval in half.
Characteristics:
•   Requires sorted data
• Much faster than linear search for large datasets
•
Time Complexity:
Case   Time Complexity
Best Case   O(1)
Average Case O(log n)
Worst Case   O(log n)
Linear Search   Binary Search
Feature
Data Requirement   Works on any data   Requires sorted data
Speed   Slower for large data Faster (logarithmic)
Implementation   Very simple   Slightly more complex
Best Use Case   Small or unsorted data Large sorted datasets
Time Complexity   O(n)   O(log n)
• Use linear search when the dataset is small or unsorted.
• Use binary search when the dataset is large and sorted for much faster performance.

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

BL-3   Case 1: Deleting a Node that has No Children
we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.
Construct a minimum spanning tree of the given graph using Prim’s
algorithm. Start from vertex 5. Show all intermediate steps.
Q6
CO-3;
Solution:   [10]
SO-1,2;
What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions

we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.
Construct a minimum spanning tree of the given graph using Prim’s
algorithm. Start from vertex 5. Show all intermediate steps.
Q6
CO-3;
Solution:   [10]
SO-1,2;
What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.

insertion, and deletion.

verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.

O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.

successor can

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.
Construct a minimum spanning tree of the given graph using Prim’s
algorithm. Start from vertex 5. Show all intermediate steps.
Q6
CO-3;
Solution:   [10]
SO-1,2;
What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

SO-1,2 ;   1. Most Suitable Data Structure: Hash Table
BL-4   Justification:
• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.
•   It provides average-case O(1) time complexity for search,
insertion, and deletion.
• This makes it ideal for systems that require quick passenger
verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.
• Other structures like arrays, lists, or trees would result in O(n) or
O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

• A priority queue automatically arranges elements based on their
priority.

priority job with minimum running time be accessed.
a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.

What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

SO-1,2 ;   1. Most Suitable Data Structure: Hash Table
BL-4   Justification:
• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.
•   It provides average-case O(1) time complexity for search,
insertion, and deletion.
• This makes it ideal for systems that require quick passenger
verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.
• Other structures like arrays, lists, or trees would result in O(n) or
O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its

Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children

predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.

What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the

verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.

O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of

node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its

Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children

predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor

successor can

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.

algorithm. Start from vertex 5. Show all intermediate steps.
Q6

Solution:   [10]
SO-1,2;
What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

1. A system needs to store passenger records with unique ticket IDs. The
system must allow constant-time lookup to check whether a passenger
exists.
2. An operating system must schedule processes such that the process with
minimum running time is scheduled first.

2=2 marks
CO-1 ;   Proper justification- 1.5 each *2= 3 marks.
SO-1,2 ;   1. Most Suitable Data Structure: Hash Table
BL-4   Justification:
• A hash table stores data in key–value pairs, where the key is the
unique ticket ID.
•   It provides average-case O(1) time complexity for search,
insertion, and deletion.
• This makes it ideal for systems that require quick passenger
verification, such as airline reservation or check-in systems.
• Other structures like arrays, lists, or trees would result in O(n) or
O(log n) lookup time, which is slower compared to a hash table.

Justification:
• A priority queue automatically arranges elements based on their
priority.
• Implemented using a min priority queue allows the highest

a.   Explain time and space complexity. Explain various asymptotic
notations used to calculate time complexity.
Solution:
Explain time and space complexity- 4 marks
Analysing an algorithm means determining the amount of resources
(such as time and memory) needed to execute it. Algorithms are
generally designed to work with an arbitrary number of inputs, so the
efficiency or complexity of an algorithm is stated in terms of time and
space complexity.
The time complexity of an algorithm is basically the running time of a
program as a function of the input size. Similarly, the space complexity
of an algorithm is the amount of computer memory that is required
during the program execution as a function of the input size.
Explain various asymptotic notations used to calculate time
complexity.- 6 marks
When we look at input sizes large enough to make only the order
of growth of the running time relevant, we are studying the
asymptotic efficiency of algorithms.
Θ –notation
we found that the worst-case running time of insertion sort is T
Q2   (n) = Θ(n2). Let us define what this notation means.
CO-1;
For a given function g(n), we denote by θ(g(n)) the set of   [10]
SO-1,2;
functions
BL-3
θ (g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c1, c2, and n0
such that 0 ≤ c1g(n) ≤ f (n) ≤ c2g(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
O-notation
The θ -notation asymptotically bounds a function from above
and below. When we have only an asymptotic upper bound, we
use O-notation.
For a given function g(n), we denote by O(g(n)) (pronounced
“big-oh of g of n” or sometimes just “oh of g of n”) the set of
functions
O(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ f (n) ≤ cg(n) for all n ≥ n0} .
Ω-notation
Just as O-notation provides an asymptotic upper bound on a
function, Ω notation provides an asymptotic lower bound. For a
given function g(n), we denote by Ω(g(n)) (pronounced “big-
omega of g of n” or sometimes just “omega of g of n”)
the set of functions
Ω(g(n)) = { f (n) : there exist positive constants c and n0 such
that 0 ≤ cg(n) ≤ f (n) for all n ≥ n0}

Explain how deletion is performed in a Binary Search Tree (BST)- 5
marks
The delete function deletes a node from the binary search tree.
CO-3;   However, utmost care should be taken that the properties of the binary
SO-1,2;   search tree are not violated and nodes are not lost in the process.   [10]
BL-3   Case 1: Deleting a Node that has No Children
we can simply remove this node by updating the link of parent node to
NULL.
Case 2: Deleting a Node with One Child
To handle this case, the node’s child is set as the child of the node’s
parent. In other words, replace the node with its child. Now, if the node
is the left child of its parent, the node’s child becomes the left child of
the
********** 5 **********
--- page 6 ---
node’s parent. Correspondingly, if the node is the right child of its
parent, the node’s child becomes the right child of the node’s parent.
Case 3: Deleting a Node with Two Children
To handle this case, replace the node’s value with its in-order
predecessor (largest value in the left sub-tree) or in-order successor
(smallest value in the right sub-tree). The in-order predecessor or the
successor can
then be deleted using any of the above cases.

a.   What is minimum spanning tree.
Construct a minimum spanning tree of the given graph using Prim’s
algorithm. Start from vertex 5. Show all intermediate steps.
Q6
CO-3;
Solution:   [10]
SO-1,2;
What is minimum spanning tree.- 4 marks
BL-3
A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph G is a sub-graph of G
which is a tree that connects all the vertices together. A graph G can
have many different spanning trees. We can assign weights to each edge
(which is a number that represents how unfavourable the edge is), and
use it to assign a weight to a spanning tree by calculating the sum of the
weights of the edges in that spanning tree. A minimum spanning tree
(MST) is defined as a spanning tree with weight less than or equal to the
weight of every other spanning tree. In other words, a minimum
spanning tree is a spanning tree that has weights associated with its
edges, and the total weight of the tree (the sum of the weights of its
edges) is at a minimum.

Algorithm: DeleteNode(head, value)
Step 1: If head is NULL:
Print "List is empty"
Exit
Step 2: Set temp = head
Set prev = NULL
Step 3: // Case 1: Node to delete is the head node
If temp != NULL AND temp.data == value:
head = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"
Exit
Step 4: // Search for the node to be deleted
While temp != NULL AND temp.data != value:
prev = temp
temp = temp.next
Step 5: // Case 2: Node not found
If temp == NULL:
Print "Node not found"
Exit
Step 6: // Case 3: Node found in middle/end
prev.next = temp.next
Free temp
Print "Node deleted"

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm for building an optimal prefix code
(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

d.   UNIT 1 theory Explain the concept of space time complexity with
example.
Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)
Q2.
What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

--- page 2 ---

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:

This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)

What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):

current = head
while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,

Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.

at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,

order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Function InsertBST(root, value)
1. If root is NULL:
Create new node with data = value
return node
2. If value < root.data:
root.left = InsertBST(root.left, value)
Else:
root.right = InsertBST(root.right, value)
2. Return root

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):
count = 0
current = head
while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.

that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
