Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item

peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):

while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

An algorithm with
𝑶(𝟏)

Space Complexity [5 Marks]
• What it is:
A measure of how the memory usage of an algorithm increases with the input size.
• How it's used:
To understand the memory footprint of an algorithm and ensure it doesn't exceed available memory for
large inputs.
• Components:
It includes both the fixed space for variables and constants and the variable space that depends on the
input size, such as for dynamic memory allocation or recursion stacks.

#define MAXSIZE 5 // Define the maximum size of the stack
int stack[MAXSIZE];

// Function to check if the stack is full
int isFull() {
return top == MAXSIZE - 1;
}
// Function to push an element onto the stack
void push(int data) {
if (isFull()) {
printf("Stack Overflow! Cannot push %d.\n", data);
} else {
top++;
stack[top] = data;
printf("%d pushed to stack.\n", data);
}
}

Q5.   [20]
A Explain the Divide and Conquer algorithm with example.
The Divide and Conquer algorithm is a problem-solving paradigm that involves breaking down a large problem
into smaller, similar subproblems, solving these subproblems independently, and then combining their solutions
to solve the original problem. This approach typically involves three main steps:
•   Divide:
The original problem is divided into several smaller subproblems that are similar in nature to the original
problem but smaller in size. This division often continues recursively until the subproblems become small
enough to be solved directly (the base case).
•   Conquer:
The subproblems are solved recursively. If a subproblem is small enough, it is solved directly. Otherwise, it
is further divided.
• Combine:
The solutions to the subproblems are combined to form the solution to the original problem.
Example: Merge Sort
Merge Sort is a classic example of a Divide and Conquer algorithm used for sorting an array.
Let's sort the array [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] using Merge Sort:
•   Divide:
o The array is split into two halves: [38, 27, 43] and [3, 9, 82, 10].
o Each half is further divided until individual elements are reached:
▪   [38, 27, 43]becomes [38], [27], [43].
▪   [3, 9, 82, 10]becomes [3], [9], [82], [10].
********** 4   **********
--- page 5 ---
o At this stage, each sub-array contains only one element, which is considered sorted.
•   Conquer:
o The single-element arrays are the base case and are inherently sorted.
• Combine:
o Sorted single-element arrays are merged back together in sorted order:
▪   [27]and [43] merge to [27, 43].
▪   [38]and [27, 43] merge to [27, 38, 43].
▪   Similarly, [3] and [9] merge to [3, 9].
▪   [82]and [10] merge to [10, 82].
▪   [3, 9]and [10, 82] merge to [3, 9, 10, 82].
o   Finally, the two sorted halves [27, 38, 43] and [3, 9, 10, 82] are merged to produce the fully sorted
array: [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].
B. “N Queen problem is Backtracking algorithm” justify with algorithmic steps
The N-Queens problem is a classic example of a backtracking algorithm because it systematically searches
for a solution by building a candidate step-by-step and "backtracks" (reverts its choices) when it determines
that a partial solution cannot be completed
. This trial-and-error approach, combined with pruning invalid paths early, is the core of backtracking.
Why N-Queens is a backtracking problem
The problem is to place N queens on NXN chessboard so that no two queens can attack each other. This
means no two queens can share the same row, column, or diagonal.
Backtracking is a natural fit for this problem for the following reasons:
•   Sequential decision-making: You can build the solution incrementally by placing one queen at a time,
typically one per row, starting from the first row.
•   Constraint satisfaction: After placing each queen, you can check if the placement is "safe" by ensuring it
doesn't conflict with any previously placed queens.
•   State-space pruning: If a queen cannot be placed in a safe position in the current row, there is no need to
explore any further placements for that row. The algorithm can "prune" this invalid path and backtrack to
the previous row to change the position of the last queen placed.
•   Systematic exploration: The method exhaustively explores the solution space by trying every possible valid
placement, guaranteeing that all solutions (or a single solution) will be found if they exist.
Backtracking algorithm steps for the N-Queens problem
The general algorithm for the N-Queens problem using backtracking involves a recursive function that attempts to
place a queen in each row.
Main function
1. Initialize an empty NXN chessboard, typically represented by a 2D array or matrix.
2. Call a recursive helper function, solveNQueens(row), starting with row = 0.
********** 5   **********
--- page 6 ---
3.   If the helper function returns a successful solution, print or store the board configuration.
Recursive helper function solveNQueens(row)
1. Base case: If row >= N, it means all N queens have been successfully placed in rows O TO n-1
. A solution has been found. Return true.
2. Recursive step: Iterate through each column from 0 to N-1 for the current row:
a. Check for safety: Check if placing a queen at board[row][column] is safe from attack by queens in
previous rows. This involves checking the current column, and both diagonals (upper-left and upper-right).
b. Place the queen (Choose): If the position is safe, place a queen at board[row][column].
c. Recur for next row (Explore): Recursively call solveNQueens(row + 1) to place the next queen.
d. Check the result:
* If the recursive call returns true, it means a full solution was found. Return true to pass the success back
up the call stack.
* If the recursive call returns false, it means a dead end was reached.
e. Remove the queen (Backtrack): Reset board[row][column] to empty. This "un-places" the queen and
backtracks to try the next possible column in the current row.
3. No solution in this row: If the loop finishes without finding a safe placement for a queen in the current
row, return false. This triggers the backtracking step in the previous recursive call.

new_node->data = new_data;

last->next = new_node;
// 6. Make the last node the previous of the new node
new_node->prev = last;
}

Genetic Algorithm [3 Marks]
Steps of a genetic algorithm
1. Initialization:
Create an initial population of candidate solutions, often represented as "chromosomes" (strings of data),
by generating them randomly.
2. Fitness Evaluation:
Score each individual in the population using a fitness function. This score represents how good a solution
is for the problem you are trying to solve.
3. Selection:
Choose parents from the current population based on their fitness. Individuals with higher fitness have a
greater chance of being selected to reproduce. Common methods include roulette wheel
selection and tournament selection.
4. Crossover (Recombination):
Create new "offspring" solutions by combining the genetic material of selected parents. This is often done
by swapping parts of the parent chromosomes at a random point.
5. Mutation:
Introduce small, random changes to the new offspring's chromosomes. This ensures genetic diversity and
prevents the algorithm from getting stuck in a local optimum.
6. Replacement:
Create the next generation by replacing the old population with the new offspring. This new population
will then go through the evaluation and selection process again.
7. Termination:
Repeat the process of evaluation, selection, crossover, and mutation until a stopping criterion is met, such
as reaching a satisfactory fitness level, a maximum number of generations, or when the population
converges.
********** 8   **********
--- page 9 ---
Application [2 marks]
Applications of genetic algorithms
•   Optimization: Finding the best solution from a large set of possibilities, such as in engineering design,
financial modeling, and hyperparameter tuning.
• Machine Learning: Used for tasks like neural network training, feature selection, and data mining.
•   Robotics: Optimizing robot behavior and motion planning.
• Computer Science: Solving complex problems like the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), scheduling, and
Sudoku puzzles.
•   Signal and Image Processing: For tasks like feature extraction and image restoration.

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:

data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********

peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm for building an optimal prefix code
(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

d.   UNIT 1 theory Explain the concept of space time complexity with
example.
Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)
Q2.
What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.

2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.

a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):

current = current.next
return count

Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]

}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)

What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
An expression tree is a binary tree used to represent arithmetic
expressions.
Internal nodes represent operators (+, -, *, /, ^, etc.).
Leaf nodes represent operands (like variables or constants).
Expression trees are useful for:
Evaluating expressions
Converting between prefix, infix, and postfix forms
Representing expressions in compilers and interpreters
Function InsertBST(root, value)
1. If root is NULL:
Create new node with data = value
return node
2. If value < root.data:
root.left = InsertBST(root.left, value)
Else:
root.right = InsertBST(root.right, value)
2. Return root

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):
count = 0
current = head
while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm

An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.

Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):

current = head
while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

weighted path length of a binary tree).

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

while current is not NULL:

current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm for building an optimal prefix code
(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

d.   UNIT 1 theory Explain the concept of space time complexity with
example.
Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)

a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node

Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)
Q2.
What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)

What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:
int a[n]; Space grows with input → O(n)
Q2.
What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Priority can be defined in two ways: higher value means higher priority
(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]
// constant time operation
}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
If you create an array of size n:

Q2.
What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.

current = current.next
return count

Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.

a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.

a.   Explain double ended queue and Priority Queue with example.
Answer:
A Double Ended Queue (Deque) is a linear data structure that allows
insertion and deletion of elements from both ends — front and rear.
Unlike a standard queue that follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO), a deque
supports operations at either end, making it more versatile. Elements can
be added or removed from the front or rear efficiently.
A priority queue is a data structure in which every element is assigned a
priority, and elements are served based on their priority rather than their
5
order of arrival. The item with the highest priority is removed first, and
in case of identical priorities, the first-in-first-out (FIFO) order is used.
How Priority Queue Works
Each element is given a priority—either explicitly (with a separate value)
or implicitly (e.g., based on value for numbers).
On insertion, the element is placed in the appropriate position according
to its priority.
On deletion, the element with the highest priority is removed first.

--- page 2 ---

(max-priority queue), or lower value means higher priority (min-priority
queue).

Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm for building an optimal prefix code
(variable-length binary codes with no code a prefix of another) for a set
of symbols with known frequencies. The goal is to minimize the total
number of bits needed to encode the symbols (equivalently, minimize the
weighted path length of a binary tree).

Space–Time Complexity is a fundamental concept in computer science
used to evaluate how efficient an algorithm is. It tells us how much time
and memory (space) an algorithm needs as the size of the input grows.
1. Time Complexity: Time complexity measures how long an algorithm
takes to run, based on the input size n, rather than actual execution time.
Example
Consider a loop:
for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
[5]

}
This loop runs n times, so time complexity is: O(n) → Linear time
2. Space Complexity: Space complexity measures how much extra
memory an algorithm uses apart from input data.
This includes: Variables, Arrays, Recursion stack, Temporary storage.
int sum = 0;   // constant memory
Space = constant → O(1)
