What is data structure?.what are its different types. Explain Abstract   [10]
a.
data type with example.
A data structure is a way of organizing, storing, and managing data so
that it can be used efficiently. A data structure decides how data is
arranged in memory and how operations like insertion, deletion, and
searching are performed.
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
Types of Data Structures
1. Primitive Data Structures
These are basic data types provided by programming languages:
Int,float,char,double
They store simple values.
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures
These are more complex and are used to store large data in an organized
way.
A. Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged sequentially.
Examples :Array, Linked List, Stack,Queue
B. Non-Linear Data Structures
Data is arranged in hierarchical or network form.
Examples:Tree,Graph
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a theoretical model for a data structure
that defines:
What operations can be performed and not How the operations are
implemented.
In other words: ADT describes the behavior, not the implementation. It
focuses on what the data type should do, not how it does it internally.
Different implementations can provide the same ADT.
Why ADT? Helps in data abstraction
• Implementation details are hidden
• Makes programs easier to maintain and modify
• Allows different internal representations
Characteristics: An ADT usually specifies:
• Data stored
• Operations allowed
• Behavior of operations
Example 1: Stack ADT
Definition: A Stack is an ADT that follows LIFO (Last In, First Out)
principle.
Operations:push(x) → insert an item
pop() → remove top item
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
peek() → view top item
isEmpty() → check if empty
ADT does not specify: Whether stack is implemented using array,
linked list, or something else.

What is the expression tree. Write an algorithm to insert an element in

Answer:
An expression tree is a binary tree used to represent arithmetic
expressions.
Internal nodes represent operators (+, -, *, /, ^, etc.).
Leaf nodes represent operands (like variables or constants).
Expression trees are useful for:
Evaluating expressions
Converting between prefix, infix, and postfix forms
Representing expressions in compilers and interpreters
Function InsertBST(root, value)
1. If root is NULL:
Create new node with data = value
return node
2. If value < root.data:
root.left = InsertBST(root.left, value)
Else:
root.right = InsertBST(root.right, value)
2. Return root

Answer:
Strictly Binary Tree (Full Binary Tree): Every node has either 0 or 2
children. No node has only one child. This means each internal node
has exactly two children, and leaves have none.
Complete Binary Tree: All levels are fully filled except possibly the last
level, which is filled from left to right without gaps. Nodes may have
zero, one, or two children at the last level, but all earlier levels are fully
populated.

What benefits do linked lists have over arrays? Write an iterative
algorithm/function for counting the number of nodes in a singly linked
list?
Linked lists have several benefits over arrays:
Dynamic Size: Linked lists can grow or shrink dynamically without
needing a predefined size, unlike arrays which require a fixed size or
costly resizing.
Efficient Insertions/Deletions: Adding or removing elements, especially
in the middle, is more efficient in linked lists since it only involves
changing pointers rather than shifting elements as in arrays.
No Memory Waste: Linked lists allocate memory as needed, avoiding
waste from over-allocation common with arrays.
Easy Memory Utilization: Linked lists can utilize memory scattered
around, whereas arrays need contiguous memory allocation.
However, linked lists have disadvantages too, like no direct indexing,
requiring sequential access.
function countNodes(head):
count = 0
current = head
while current is not NULL:
count = count + 1
current = current.next
return count

How are Binary trees represented in computer memory? Explain with
example. Construct a binary search tree using following elements
arranged in array as shown: 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 9,
11, 6, 18
Answer:
Binary trees are represented in computer memory using two primary
methods: linked representation, which uses nodes with pointers to child
nodes, and sequential (or array) representation, which stores nodes in a
single array. The linked representation uses structures that contain the
node's data along with left and right pointers to other nodes, while the
array representation uses indices to define the parent-child
relationships.
1. Linked representation Concept: Each node is a separate structure
(or object) that contains three parts:A field for the data.A "left"
pointer (or address) to the left child node.A "right" pointer to the
right child node.
2. Sequential (Array) representation Concept: The tree is stored in
a one-dimensional array, and the parent-child relationships are
determined by the indices of the array elements.
********** 16 **********
--- page 17 ---
How it works: The root node is typically stored at index 0 or index 1.
For a node at index i (assuming the root is at index 0): Its left child is at
index 2i+1. Its right child is at index 2i+2. To find the parent of a node
at index k, you can use the formula: floor(k/2) if the root is at index 1,
or (floor((k-1)/2)) if the root is at index 0. 13, 13, 3, 4, 12, 12,14, 10, 5,

Q1
Answer briefly:
a.   Define Algorithm. Explain its features and characteristics with the help
of a suitable example.
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or a set of rules used to solve
a problem, perform a computation, or achieve a specific outcome. It is
essentially a systematic plan, expressed in a sequence of well-defined
steps, designed to accomplish a particular task when executed.
Algorithms can range from simple mathematical calculations to
complex data-processing routines, and they form the foundation of
computer programming and problem-solving in various fields.
Key Features and Characteristics of Algorithms
5
1. Finiteness: An algorithm must always terminate after a finite
number of steps. It should not go into an infinite loop, ensuring
the solution is reached within a reasonable time frame.
2. Definiteness: Each step in an algorithm must be clear and
unambiguous. There should be no confusion or room for
interpretation at any stage.
3. Input: An algorithm should have well-defined inputs. These
inputs are the data that the algorithm processes to generate the
desired output.
4. Output: An algorithm must produce at least one output,
providing a solution to the problem or a response based on the
given inputs.
5. Effectiveness: Each step of an algorithm should be basic enough
to be carried out, in principle, by a person using a pen and paper,
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
or by a computer. This characteristic ensures the algorithm is
feasible.
6. Language Independence: An algorithm is not bound to a
specific programming language. It’s a logical sequence that can
be implemented in any language.
b.   Define Recursion. Explain three types of recursion using suitable
examples
Recursion is a programming technique where a function calls itself in order to
solve a problem. Each recursive call breaks down the problem into smaller
subproblems, and the process continues until it reaches a "base case" (a simple
case with a known solution). Recursion is particularly useful in problems that
can be divided into similar subproblems, like in the case of factorials, Fibonacci
numbers, or tree traversal.
Types of Recursion
1. Direct Recursion
5
In direct recursion, a function calls itself directly within its own
code. This is the simplest form of recursion, where the function
solves the problem by repeatedly calling itself with modified
arguments until it reaches the base case.
Indirect Recursion
In indirect recursion, a function does not call itself directly but instead
calls another function, which then calls the original function. This form
of recursion involves two or more functions that call each other in a
cyclic manner.
Tail Recursion
In tail recursion, the recursive call is the last operation in the function.
There is no additional work required after the recursive call. This type
of recursion is optimized by some compilers, which reuses the current
function stack frame for the next recursive call, reducing memory
usage.

d.   What do you understand by hashing? Give the properties of the good hash
function.
Hashing is a process that converts input data of any size into a fixed-
size string of characters, which is typically a sequence of numbers and
letters. This output is called a hash value or hash code. Hashing is
widely used in various applications, including data integrity
verification, password storage, and efficient data retrieval in hash
tables.
Properties of a Good Hash Function
1. Deterministic: The same input should always produce the same
hash output. This is crucial for consistency, especially when
verifying data integrity.
2. Fast Computation: The hash function should be able to
compute the hash value quickly, allowing for efficient data   5
processing and retrieval.
3. Uniform Distribution: The hash values should be uniformly
distributed across the output space. This minimizes the chance of
collisions (different inputs producing the same hash value),
ensuring that the hash table remains efficient.
4. Pre-image Resistance: Given a hash output, it should be
computationally infeasible to reverse-engineer the original input.
This property is important for security, particularly in password
hashing.
5. Second Pre-image Resistance: Given an input and its hash, it
should be hard to find another input that produces the same hash.
This further reduces the likelihood of collisions.
6. Collision Resistance: It should be difficult to find two different
inputs that hash to the same value. A good hash function
minimizes the occurrence of collisions.
7. Avalanche Effect: A small change in the input (even a single
bit) should produce a significantly different hash output. This
********** 3 **********
--- page 4 ---
property ensures that similar inputs do not lead to similar hash
values.
These properties make hashing functions suitable for various
applications, particularly in cryptography and data integrity. Examples
of widely used hash functions include SHA-256, MD5, and SHA-1
(although MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer considered secure).
a.   Explain the criteria for choosing the appropriate algorithm to solve a
particular problem. List down the categories of algorithms.
Choosing the appropriate algorithm to solve a particular problem
involves several criteria that ensure efficiency, effectiveness, and
suitability for the specific context of the problem. Here are the key
criteria to consider:
Criteria for Choosing an Algorithm
1. Correctness: The algorithm must produce the correct output for
all valid inputs. It should solve the problem as intended without
any errors.
2. Efficiency:
o Time Complexity: Analyze the algorithm's execution
time based on the input size. Prefer algorithms with lower
time complexity (e.g., O(n), O(log n)) for larger datasets.
o Space Complexity: Consider the amount of memory
required by the algorithm. A good algorithm should use
memory efficiently.
3. Scalability: The algorithm should perform well as the input size
increases. It should handle larger datasets without a significant   10
drop in performance.
Q2
4. Simplicity and Clarity: An algorithm should be easy to
understand, implement, and maintain. Complex algorithms can   10
lead to bugs and difficulties in debugging.
5. Robustness: The algorithm should be able to handle unexpected
or edge case inputs gracefully without crashing.
6. Generality: Consider whether the algorithm can be applied to a
broader class of problems or if it is specific to the current
problem. A more general algorithm may save time in future
applications.
7. Parallelizability: If the problem can be solved faster using
parallel processing, consider algorithms that can be easily
divided into smaller tasks.
8. Optimality: In some cases, you may need to choose the most
optimal algorithm for a given context, especially when dealing
with performance-critical applications.
Categories of Algorithms
Algorithms can be categorized in various ways, including:
1. Based on Problem Type:
o Sorting Algorithms: (e.g., Quick Sort, Merge Sort,
Bubble Sort)
********** 4 **********
--- page 5 ---
o Searching Algorithms: (e.g., Binary Search, Linear
Search)
o Graph Algorithms: (e.g., Dijkstra’s Algorithm,
Kruskal’s Algorithm)
o Dynamic Programming Algorithms: (e.g., Fibonacci
sequence, Knapsack problem)
o Greedy Algorithms: (e.g., Prim’s Algorithm, Huffman
Coding)
2. Based on Technique:
o Divide and Conquer: (e.g., Merge Sort, Quick Sort)
o Dynamic Programming: (e.g., Longest Common
Subsequence)
o Backtracking: (e.g., N-Queens problem, Sudoku solver)
o Brute Force: (e.g., Exhaustive search)
3. Based on Data Structure:
o Tree Algorithms: (e.g., Traversal algorithms like In-
order, Pre-order)
o Hashing Algorithms: (e.g., Hash tables for fast data
retrieval)
o Heap Algorithms: (e.g., Heap Sort, Priority Queue)
4. Based on Complexity:
o Polynomial Time Algorithms: (e.g., O(n^2), O(n log n))
o Exponential Time Algorithms: (e.g., O(2^n), O(n!))
o Approximation Algorithms: Useful for NP-hard
problems where finding an exact solution is impractical.
5. Based on Paradigm:
o Randomized Algorithms: Use randomness to make
decisions during execution (e.g., Randomized Quick
Sort).
o Heuristic Algorithms: Aim for good enough solutions in
b.   a reasonable time frame (e.g., Genetic Algorithms,
Simulated Annealing)
Write and explain the algorithm for inserting and deleting a node in the
doubly linked list at a position
(1)Beginning (2) End 3) After a specific node
A doubly linked list (DLL) is a data structure consisting of nodes,
where each node contains three fields: data, a pointer to the next node,
and a pointer to the previous node. This structure allows for efficient
insertion and deletion of nodes from both ends and at any specific
position in the list.
Algorithm for Inserting a Node
1. Insertion at the Beginning
Algorithm Steps:
1. Create a new node and allocate memory for it.
2. Set the data of the new node.
3.   If the list is empty:
o Set the new node's next pointer to NULL.
o Set the new node's prev pointer to NULL.
4.   If the list is not empty:
o Set the next pointer of the new node to point to the current
head of the list.
********** 5 **********
--- page 6 ---
o Set the prev pointer of the current head to point to the new
node.
2. Insertion at the End
Algorithm Steps:
1. Create a new node and allocate memory for it.
2. Set the data of the new node.
3.   If the list is empty:
o Set the new node's next and prev pointers to NULL and
update the head.
4.   If the list is not empty:
o Traverse to the last node (where next is NULL).
o Set the next pointer of the last node to point to the new
node.
o Set the prev pointer of the new node to point to the last
node.
o Set the next pointer of the new node to NULL.
3. Insertion After a Specific Node
Algorithm Steps:
1. Create a new node and allocate memory for it.
2. Set the data of the new node.
3. Check if the specific node (after which we want to insert) is NULL. If it
is, return without inserting.
4. Set the next pointer of the new node to the next pointer of the
specific node.
5. Set the prev pointer of the new node to point to the specific node.
6. Update the next pointer of the specific node to point to the new
node.
7.   If the new node is not the last node, update the prev pointer of the
node that follows the specific node to point to the new node.

distance = map with all nodes as keys and infinity as values

// Create a priority queue (min-heap)

priority_queue.push(neighbor, new_distance)
return distance // Returns the shortest distances from the source to all

a.   You are designing a web browser navigation system that allows users to
navigate their browsing history. The system needs to support the
following operations:
1. Navigate to a new page: When a user visits a new webpage,
it should be added to the browsing history.
2. Return to the previous page: Allow the user to return to the
previous page they were viewing.
3. Go forward to the next page: After going back, allow the user
to move forward to the next page in the history.   10
4. Clear history: Clear the entire browsing history.
Which data structure(s) would you use to manage the browsing
history, and why? Discuss how the operations would be
implemented, showing the algorithm and analyse each
operation's time and space complexity.
Answer:
For managing the web browser navigation system, the following data
Q6   structures can be utilized:
1. Stack for Back and Forward Navigation:
o Reasoning: A stack is ideal for managing the browsing
history in terms of "back" and "forward" operations. When a
user navigates to a new page, the current page is pushed
onto the "back" stack. If the user goes back, the current
page is pushed onto the "forward" stack and the previous
page is popped from the "back" stack.
o Time Complexity:   10
▪   Navigate to a new page: O(1) - Pushing the current
page onto the "back" stack is constant time.
▪ Go back to the previous page: O(1) - Popping from
the "back" stack and pushing onto the "forward"
stack are constant time operations.
▪ Go forward to the next page: O(1) - Popping from the
"forward" stack and pushing onto the "back" stack
are constant time.
▪   Clear history: O(1) - Clearing the stacks can be done
in constant time by reinitializing them.
********** 10 **********
--- page 11 ---
o Space Complexity: O(n) - Space usage is linear with the
number of pages visited.
Conclusion: Using two stacks (one for "back" and one for "forward")
efficiently manages the browsing history, supporting quick navigation with
minimal overhead.

III. 1. Adjacency Matrix (2.5 marks)   5
Description: This is a 2D array where each cell [i][j] indicates whether there is an edge
between vertex i and vertex j. For example, if there's an edge, the cell will have a value of 1 (or
the weight of the edge), and if not, it will be 0.
Advantages:
Simple to implement and understand.
Efficient for checking if an edge exists between two vertices (O(1) time).
Disadvantages:
Uses a lot of memory, especially for sparse graphs (O(V²) space).
Inefficient for adding or removing edges.
2. Adjacency List (2.5 marks)
Description: This is an array of lists. Each index in the array represents a vertex, and the list at
that index contains all the vertices it is connected to.
Advantages:
Page 2 of 17

More memory-efficient for sparse graphs (O(V + E) space).
Faster to iterate through neighbors of a vertex.
Disadvantages:
Checking for the existence of an edge between two vertices can take longer (O(V) time in the
worst case).
Slightly more complex to implement compared to an adjacency matrix.

algorithm consists of two main phases:

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary

Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

III. 1. Adjacency Matrix (2.5 marks)   5
Description: This is a 2D array where each cell [i][j] indicates whether there is an edge
between vertex i and vertex j. For example, if there's an edge, the cell will have a value of 1 (or
the weight of the edge), and if not, it will be 0.
Advantages:
Simple to implement and understand.
Efficient for checking if an edge exists between two vertices (O(1) time).
Disadvantages:
Uses a lot of memory, especially for sparse graphs (O(V²) space).
Inefficient for adding or removing edges.
2. Adjacency List (2.5 marks)
Description: This is an array of lists. Each index in the array represents a vertex, and the list at
that index contains all the vertices it is connected to.
Advantages:
Page 2 of 17

More memory-efficient for sparse graphs (O(V + E) space).
Faster to iterate through neighbors of a vertex.
Disadvantages:
Checking for the existence of an edge between two vertices can take longer (O(V) time in the
worst case).
Slightly more complex to implement compared to an adjacency matrix.
IV. Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that efficiently sorts a dataset by dividing it into   5
smaller subarrays, sorting those subarrays, and then merging them back together. The
algorithm consists of two main phases:
1. Divide: Split the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element.
2. Conquer (Merge): Merge the subarrays back together in sorted order.
Steps of the Merge Sort Algorithm
1. If the array has one or zero elements, it is already sorted. Return it.
2. Divide the array into two halves.
3. Recursively apply merge sort to both halves.
4. Merge the two sorted halves into a single sorted array.

Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17

For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.

Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

def partition(array, low, high):
pivot = array[high]
i = low - 1
for j in range(low, high):

i += 1
array[i], array[j] = array[j], array[i]
array[i+1], array[high] = array[high], array[i+1]
return i+1

1. Suitable Data Structure: Stack (2 Marks)   10
Justification: A stack is the most suitable data structure for implementing an "Undo"
feature in a text editor because:
LIFO (Last In, First Out): Stacks follow the LIFO principle, meaning the most recent
action can be undone first. This is precisely the behavior needed for undoing text edits,
where the last change made is the first one to revert.
Simple Operations: Stacks allow for efficient push and pop operations, which
correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.
Dynamic Size: Using a linked list to implement the stack allows for a dynamic size,
accommodating an arbitrary number of actions without worrying about pre-allocation
or resizing issues associated with arrays.

2. [2.5] marks for each real-word application explanation. (any two)   5
Social Media Platforms: Data structures like graphs are essential in social media
applications. Users can be represented as nodes, while connections (friends or
followers) can be represented as edges. This allows for efficient management of
relationships, enabling features like friend suggestions, news feed algorithms, and
community detection.
Databases: Data structures such as B-trees and hash tables are widely used in
database management systems. B-trees help in maintaining sorted data and allow for
efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations. Hash tables enable quick data
retrieval by mapping keys to values, making them ideal for applications requiring fast
access to data, like caching user sessions in web applications.
Search Engines: Data structures like inverted indexes and tries are vital in search
engines. An inverted index maps keywords to their locations in documents, allowing
for fast and efficient full-text searches. Tries are used for autocomplete features,
enabling quick suggestions as users type queries.
Network Routing: Data structures such as priority queues and graphs are used in
network routing algorithms. For example, Dijkstra’s algorithm utilizes a priority
queue to find the shortest path between nodes in a network, which is crucial for
efficient data transmission and reducing latency in communication networks.

retrieval by mapping keys to values, making them ideal for applications requiring fast
access to data, like caching user sessions in web applications.

enabling quick suggestions as users type queries.
Network Routing: Data structures such as priority queues and graphs are used in
network routing algorithms. For example, Dijkstra’s algorithm utilizes a priority
queue to find the shortest path between nodes in a network, which is crucial for
efficient data transmission and reducing latency in communication networks.

IV. Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that efficiently sorts a dataset by dividing it into   5
smaller subarrays, sorting those subarrays, and then merging them back together. The
algorithm consists of two main phases:
1. Divide: Split the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element.
2. Conquer (Merge): Merge the subarrays back together in sorted order.
Steps of the Merge Sort Algorithm
1. If the array has one or zero elements, it is already sorted. Return it.
2. Divide the array into two halves.

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

1. Suitable Data Structure: Stack (2 Marks)   10
Justification: A stack is the most suitable data structure for implementing an "Undo"
feature in a text editor because:
LIFO (Last In, First Out): Stacks follow the LIFO principle, meaning the most recent
action can be undone first. This is precisely the behavior needed for undoing text edits,
where the last change made is the first one to revert.
Simple Operations: Stacks allow for efficient push and pop operations, which
correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.
Dynamic Size: Using a linked list to implement the stack allows for a dynamic size,
accommodating an arbitrary number of actions without worrying about pre-allocation
or resizing issues associated with arrays.

2. [2.5] marks for each real-word application explanation. (any two)   5
Social Media Platforms: Data structures like graphs are essential in social media
applications. Users can be represented as nodes, while connections (friends or
followers) can be represented as edges. This allows for efficient management of
relationships, enabling features like friend suggestions, news feed algorithms, and
community detection.
Databases: Data structures such as B-trees and hash tables are widely used in
database management systems. B-trees help in maintaining sorted data and allow for
efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations. Hash tables enable quick data
retrieval by mapping keys to values, making them ideal for applications requiring fast
access to data, like caching user sessions in web applications.
Search Engines: Data structures like inverted indexes and tries are vital in search
engines. An inverted index maps keywords to their locations in documents, allowing
for fast and efficient full-text searches. Tries are used for autocomplete features,
enabling quick suggestions as users type queries.
Network Routing: Data structures such as priority queues and graphs are used in
network routing algorithms. For example, Dijkstra’s algorithm utilizes a priority
queue to find the shortest path between nodes in a network, which is crucial for
efficient data transmission and reducing latency in communication networks.

III. 1. Adjacency Matrix (2.5 marks)   5
Description: This is a 2D array where each cell [i][j] indicates whether there is an edge
between vertex i and vertex j. For example, if there's an edge, the cell will have a value of 1 (or
the weight of the edge), and if not, it will be 0.
Advantages:
Simple to implement and understand.
Efficient for checking if an edge exists between two vertices (O(1) time).
Disadvantages:
Uses a lot of memory, especially for sparse graphs (O(V²) space).
Inefficient for adding or removing edges.
2. Adjacency List (2.5 marks)
Description: This is an array of lists. Each index in the array represents a vertex, and the list at
that index contains all the vertices it is connected to.
Advantages:
Page 2 of 17
--- page 3 ---
More memory-efficient for sparse graphs (O(V + E) space).
Faster to iterate through neighbors of a vertex.
Disadvantages:
Checking for the existence of an edge between two vertices can take longer (O(V) time in the
worst case).
Slightly more complex to implement compared to an adjacency matrix.
IV. Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that efficiently sorts a dataset by dividing it into   5
smaller subarrays, sorting those subarrays, and then merging them back together. The
algorithm consists of two main phases:
1. Divide: Split the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element.
2. Conquer (Merge): Merge the subarrays back together in sorted order.
Steps of the Merge Sort Algorithm
1. If the array has one or zero elements, it is already sorted. Return it.
2. Divide the array into two halves.
3. Recursively apply merge sort to both halves.
4. Merge the two sorted halves into a single sorted array.

Right Half: Split into [90, 27] and [72, 18].

5. Merging the Right Half:
[90] and [27] merge to [27, 90].
[72] and [18] merge to [18, 72].
Merging both results: [18, 27, 72, 90].
6. Final Merge:
Merge the sorted left half [9, 39, 45, 81] and the sorted right half [18, 27, 72, 90] to get
the final sorted array:
Sorted Array: [9, 18, 27, 39, 45, 72, 81, 90].

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

def partition(array, low, high):
pivot = array[high]
i = low - 1
for j in range(low, high):
if array[j] <= pivot:
i += 1
array[i], array[j] = array[j], array[i]
array[i+1], array[high] = array[high], array[i+1]
return i+1
def quicksort(array, low=0, high=None):

1. Suitable Data Structure: Stack (2 Marks)   10
Justification: A stack is the most suitable data structure for implementing an "Undo"
feature in a text editor because:
LIFO (Last In, First Out): Stacks follow the LIFO principle, meaning the most recent
action can be undone first. This is precisely the behavior needed for undoing text edits,
where the last change made is the first one to revert.
Simple Operations: Stacks allow for efficient push and pop operations, which
correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.
Dynamic Size: Using a linked list to implement the stack allows for a dynamic size,
accommodating an arbitrary number of actions without worrying about pre-allocation
or resizing issues associated with arrays.

Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

feature in a text editor because:

correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.

or resizing issues associated with arrays.

III. 1. Adjacency Matrix (2.5 marks)   5
Description: This is a 2D array where each cell [i][j] indicates whether there is an edge
between vertex i and vertex j. For example, if there's an edge, the cell will have a value of 1 (or
the weight of the edge), and if not, it will be 0.
Advantages:
Simple to implement and understand.
Efficient for checking if an edge exists between two vertices (O(1) time).
Disadvantages:
Uses a lot of memory, especially for sparse graphs (O(V²) space).
Inefficient for adding or removing edges.

Description: This is an array of lists. Each index in the array represents a vertex, and the list at
that index contains all the vertices it is connected to.
Advantages:
Page 2 of 17

More memory-efficient for sparse graphs (O(V + E) space).
Faster to iterate through neighbors of a vertex.
Disadvantages:

worst case).
Slightly more complex to implement compared to an adjacency matrix.
IV. Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that efficiently sorts a dataset by dividing it into   5
smaller subarrays, sorting those subarrays, and then merging them back together. The
algorithm consists of two main phases:
1. Divide: Split the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element.
2. Conquer (Merge): Merge the subarrays back together in sorted order.
Steps of the Merge Sort Algorithm
1. If the array has one or zero elements, it is already sorted. Return it.
2. Divide the array into two halves.
3. Recursively apply merge sort to both halves.
4. Merge the two sorted halves into a single sorted array.

Right Half: Split into [90, 27] and [72, 18].

[90] and [27] merge to [27, 90].
[72] and [18] merge to [18, 72].
Merging both results: [18, 27, 72, 90].
6. Final Merge:
Merge the sorted left half [9, 39, 45, 81] and the sorted right half [18, 27, 72, 90] to get
the final sorted array:
Sorted Array: [9, 18, 27, 39, 45, 72, 81, 90].

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

def partition(array, low, high):
pivot = array[high]
i = low - 1
for j in range(low, high):
if array[j] <= pivot:
i += 1
array[i], array[j] = array[j], array[i]
array[i+1], array[high] = array[high], array[i+1]
return i+1
def quicksort(array, low=0, high=None):

1. Suitable Data Structure: Stack (2 Marks)   10
Justification: A stack is the most suitable data structure for implementing an "Undo"
feature in a text editor because:
LIFO (Last In, First Out): Stacks follow the LIFO principle, meaning the most recent
action can be undone first. This is precisely the behavior needed for undoing text edits,
where the last change made is the first one to revert.
Simple Operations: Stacks allow for efficient push and pop operations, which
correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.
Dynamic Size: Using a linked list to implement the stack allows for a dynamic size,
accommodating an arbitrary number of actions without worrying about pre-allocation
or resizing issues associated with arrays.

2. [2.5] marks for each real-word application explanation. (any two)   5
Social Media Platforms: Data structures like graphs are essential in social media
applications. Users can be represented as nodes, while connections (friends or
followers) can be represented as edges. This allows for efficient management of
relationships, enabling features like friend suggestions, news feed algorithms, and
community detection.
Databases: Data structures such as B-trees and hash tables are widely used in
database management systems. B-trees help in maintaining sorted data and allow for
efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations. Hash tables enable quick data
retrieval by mapping keys to values, making them ideal for applications requiring fast
access to data, like caching user sessions in web applications.
Search Engines: Data structures like inverted indexes and tries are vital in search
engines. An inverted index maps keywords to their locations in documents, allowing
for fast and efficient full-text searches. Tries are used for autocomplete features,
enabling quick suggestions as users type queries.
Network Routing: Data structures such as priority queues and graphs are used in
network routing algorithms. For example, Dijkstra’s algorithm utilizes a priority
queue to find the shortest path between nodes in a network, which is crucial for
efficient data transmission and reducing latency in communication networks.

IV. Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that efficiently sorts a dataset by dividing it into   5

algorithm consists of two main phases:
1. Divide: Split the array into two halves until each subarray contains a single element.

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

1. Allocate three marks each for representing and explaining the array and linked list   10
representations. Additionally, allocate two marks each for describing the advantages
and disadvantages of each representation.
Array Representation
In an array representation of a binary tree, the tree nodes are stored in a sequential
manner. The root node is placed at the first index, and the children of each node are
placed at specific indices based on their parent’s index.
Indexing Rules:
Page 8 of 17
--- page 9 ---
The root node is at index 0.
For any node at index (i):
The left child is at index (2i + 1).
The right child is at index (2i + 2).
Advantages:
1. Direct Access: Nodes can be accessed directly using their indices, which makes
traversal operations faster.
2. Memory Efficiency: For complete binary trees, arrays are memory efficient as there
are no unused spaces.
Disadvantages:
1. Wasted Space: For sparse trees, many array elements may remain unused, leading
to memory wastage.
2. Fixed Size: The size of the array needs to be defined initially, which can be limiting
if the tree grows beyond the allocated size.
Linked List Representation
In a linked list representation, each node contains data and pointers to its left and right
children. This is typically implemented using a structure or class with three fields: data,
left pointer, and right pointer.
Advantages:
1. Dynamic Size: The tree can grow and shrink dynamically as nodes are added or
removed.
2. Memory Utilization: Only the required memory is allocated, avoiding wastage.
Disadvantages:
1. Pointer Overhead: Each node requires additional memory for storing pointers,
which can be significant for large trees.
2. Traversal Complexity: Accessing nodes is slower compared to arrays as it requires
following pointers.
Summary
Page 9 of 17
--- page 10 ---
Array Representation: Efficient for complete binary trees with direct access to
nodes but can waste space for sparse trees and has a fixed size.
Linked List Representation: Flexible and memory-efficient for dynamic trees but has
pointer overhead and slower access times.
2. Linear Probing with example- 5 marks   10
Linear probing resolves collisions by checking the next available slot in the hash table
sequentially until an empty slot is found. This method utilizes the formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i)modTable Size
where ii is the number of attempts made to find an open slot (starting from 0).
Quadratic Probing with example- 5 marks
Quadratic probing is a collision resolution technique used in open addressing for hash
tables. When a collision occurs (i.e., when two keys hash to the same index), quadratic
probing finds the next available slot using a quadratic function.
Key Concepts
Hash Function: A function that computes an index for a given key.
Collision: Occurs when two keys hash to the same index.
Quadratic Probing Formula:
\text{New Index} = ( \text{Hash(key)} + i^2 ) \mod \text{Table Size}
New Index=(Hash(key)+i2)modTable Size
Here, ii represents the number of attempts made to resolve the collision, starting
from 00.
How It Works
1. Calculate the Initial Index: Use the hash function to determine the initial index for
the key.
2. Collision Detection: If the calculated index is already occupied, increment ii and
calculate the next index using the quadratic probing formula.
3. Repeat: Continue checking the next index until an empty slot is found.
4. Insertion: Place the key in the found empty slot.

def partition(array, low, high):
pivot = array[high]
i = low - 1
for j in range(low, high):
if array[j] <= pivot:
i += 1
array[i], array[j] = array[j], array[i]
array[i+1], array[high] = array[high], array[i+1]
return i+1

Justification: A stack is the most suitable data structure for implementing an "Undo"
feature in a text editor because:
LIFO (Last In, First Out): Stacks follow the LIFO principle, meaning the most recent
action can be undone first. This is precisely the behavior needed for undoing text edits,
where the last change made is the first one to revert.
Simple Operations: Stacks allow for efficient push and pop operations, which
correspond to recording an action and undoing it, respectively.
Dynamic Size: Using a linked list to implement the stack allows for a dynamic size,
accommodating an arbitrary number of actions without worrying about pre-allocation
or resizing issues associated with arrays.

Social Media Platforms: Data structures like graphs are essential in social media
applications. Users can be represented as nodes, while connections (friends or
followers) can be represented as edges. This allows for efficient management of
relationships, enabling features like friend suggestions, news feed algorithms, and
community detection.
Databases: Data structures such as B-trees and hash tables are widely used in
database management systems. B-trees help in maintaining sorted data and allow for
efficient insertion, deletion, and search operations. Hash tables enable quick data
retrieval by mapping keys to values, making them ideal for applications requiring fast
access to data, like caching user sessions in web applications.
Search Engines: Data structures like inverted indexes and tries are vital in search
engines. An inverted index maps keywords to their locations in documents, allowing
for fast and efficient full-text searches. Tries are used for autocomplete features,
enabling quick suggestions as users type queries.
Network Routing: Data structures such as priority queues and graphs are used in
network routing algorithms. For example, Dijkstra’s algorithm utilizes a priority
queue to find the shortest path between nodes in a network, which is crucial for
efficient data transmission and reducing latency in communication networks.

a.   What is ADT? Define the Pointer Data type and its types. Explain its
arithmetic and drawbacks.
An Abstract Data Type (ADT) is a data structure that is defined by its
behavior (semantics) from the point of view of a user, rather than its
implementation. ADTs specify the types of operations that can be
performed on data, but not how these operations are implemented. This
abstraction allows users to focus on what the data structure does, not
how it does it.
Some common examples of ADTs include:
List: Supports operations like insertion, deletion, and traversal.
Queue: Supports enqueue, dequeue, and other related operations.
Stack: Supports push, pop, and peeking operations.
Pointer Arithmetic
Pointer arithmetic refers to operations performed on pointers. Common   5
1,2,2
operations include incrementing/decrementing pointers, and adding or
subtracting integers to/from pointers. Pointer arithmetic is done based
on the size of the data type the pointer refers to.
Operations:
Increment (++): Moves the pointer to the next memory location based
on the size of the data type.
• Decrement (--): Moves the pointer to the previous memory location.
• Addition/Subtraction (+, -): You can add or subtract an integer value
to/from a pointer. The pointer will move forward/backward by the given
number of data units.
Drawbacks of Pointers
Complexity: Pointers can make the code more difficult to understand and
maintain, especially for beginner programmers. Managing memory manually
using pointers can lead to errors.
********** 1 **********
--- page 2 ---
Dangling/Wild Pointers: If memory that a pointer refers to is deallocated
(freed) but the pointer is still used, it can lead to unpredictable behavior or
crashes.
Memory Leaks: If memory is allocated dynamically but not properly
deallocated, it can cause memory leaks, where memory that is no longer
needed is not released.
Segmentation Faults: Incorrect use of pointers, such as dereferencing a null
or dangling pointer, can lead to segmentation faults, causing a program to
crash.
Security Issues: Pointers can introduce security vulnerabilities, such as buffer
overflows, which can be exploited by attackers to execute malicious code.
b.   Recursion Definition
Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself to solve a
smaller instance of the same problem until it reaches a base case. The
process continues until a predefined condition, called the base case, is
met, which prevents infinite recursion and stops the function from
calling itself.
Recursion is widely used in problems that can be broken down into
simpler subproblems of the same type, such as tree traversals, factorials,
and sorting algorithms like merge sort and quicksort.
Types of Recursion
1. Direct Recursion
2. Indirect Recursion
3. Tail Recursion   5
2,2,3
Direct Recursion
In direct recursion, a function directly calls itself. It solves a problem
by dividing it into smaller instances of the same problem and calling
itself repeatedly.
Example: Factorial of a number
The factorial of a number n is the product of all integers from 1 to n.
Mathematically, it's defined as:
In indirect recursion, a function does not directly call itself, but calls
another function that eventually leads back to the original function,
forming a loop of function calls.
Example: Two functions calling each other
In tail recursion, the recursive call is the last operation in the function. This
means that no further computation is needed after the recursive call. Tail
recursion can be optimized by the compiler into an iterative loop, which
makes it more efficient in terms of memory.

efficiency of an algorithm, particularly in terms of time complexity or

or space grows as n→∞. It helps abstract away constants and lower-

Depth-First Search (DFS)
1. Start from a given node (usually the starting node is chosen or
specified).
2. Visit the node and mark it as visited.
3. Recursively visit all unvisited neighbors of the current node.
4. Once all neighbors are visited, backtrack to the previous node
and continue the process.
The DFS traversal can be implemented using a stack or recursively by
function calls.
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
1. Start from a given node.
2. Visit the node, mark it as visited, and enqueue it to a queue.
3. Dequeue a node, visit all its unvisited neighbors, mark them as
visited, and enqueue them.
4. Repeat the process until the queue is empty.
If you provide the graph details, I can work through the specific
traversal orders for DFS and BFS based on that graph’s structure.
Depth-First Search (DFS)
DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking.
For the graph, starting from node A:
1. Start at A.
2. Visit B (as it’s the first adjacent node of A).
3. Visit E (adjacent to B).
4. Visit H (adjacent to E).
5. No unvisited neighbors for H, so backtrack to E.
6. Backtrack to B, check other neighbors.
7. Visit C (another neighbor of A).
8. Visit D (adjacent to C).
9. Visit G (adjacent to D).
10. Visit I (adjacent to G).
11. Backtrack and explore any remaining nodes (there are none left).
DFS traversal order: A → B → E → H → C → D → G → I
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
BFS explores all neighbors at the present depth before moving on to
nodes at the next depth level. Starting from A:
1. Start at A.
2. Visit all neighbors of A: B and C.
3. Visit all neighbors of B and C: E, D.
4. Visit all neighbors of E and D: H, G.
********** 6 **********
--- page 7 ---
5. Visit all neighbors of H and G: I.
BFS traversal order: A → B → C → E → D → H → G → I

5. Using a Queue:
o Reasoning: A Queue is ideal for managing notifications that

Notifications are added to the back of the queue and
********** 9 **********

delivered from the front, ensuring that they are processed in
the correct sequence.
o Implementation:
1. Send a new notification: O(1) - Adding a notification
to the back of the queue is constant time.
2. Deliver notifications: O(1) - Retrieving and removing
the front notification is constant time.
3. View notification history: O(n) - Iterating through the
queue to view past notifications is linear time.
4. Clear old notifications: O(1) - Clearing the entire
queue is constant time, but selectively removing old
notifications might require iterating through the
queue.
o Space Complexity: O(n) - The space required is linear with the
number of notifications.
6. Using an ArrayList:
o Reasoning: An ArrayList allows for easy access to any
notification, making it useful for storing and viewing
notification history. However, it doesn't enforce any specific
order for processing.
o Implementation:
1. Send a new notification: O(1) - Adding a notification
to the end of the ArrayList is typically constant time.
2. Deliver notifications: O(1) - Accessing the first
notification is constant time, but removing it could be
O(n) due to shifting.
3. View notification history: O(1) - Random access
allows viewing any notification instantly.
4. Clear old notifications: O(n) - Removing elements
from the list involves shifting elements, which is linear
time.
o Space Complexity: O(n) - The space required is linear with the
number of notifications.
Conclusion:
7. Queue: A queue is the better choice if the main requirement is to
deliver notifications in a strict FIFO order. It provides efficient
handling of the notification delivery process and ensures that
notifications are processed in the correct sequence.
8. ArrayList: An ArrayList is more flexible if the system needs to support
random access to notifications or if users frequently review and
interact with their notification history. However, it may require
additional management to handle the sequential delivery of
notifications.

III. 1. Concept of Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) – (2 marks)   5
A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) is a tree that connects all the vertices in a graph using the
smallest possible total edge weight. It is formed from an undirected, weighted graph and has no
cycles.
2. Difference between MST and a general spanning tree – (1.5 marks)
A general spanning tree connects all vertices without any cycles but does not necessarily
minimize the total edge weight. An MST, on the other hand, always has the smallest possible
total edge weight among all spanning trees.
3. Practical significance and real-world example – (1.5 marks)
The MST is important in applications like network design, where the goal is to connect
locations with the least cost. For example, an MST can help in laying out the most cost-
efficient road network connecting cities.

1. Concept of Priority queue, difference, real life scenario- 5 marks   10
APQ, DPQ – 5 marks
Concept of a Priority Queue: A priority queue is an abstract data type that is similar to
a regular queue, but with an important distinction: each element in a priority queue has
an associated priority. In a priority queue, elements with higher priority are served (or
dequeued) before elements with lower priority, regardless of their order of insertion.
Difference from a Regular Queue:
a. Regular Queue: Follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle. The element that
has been in the queue the longest is always the first to be dequeued.
b. Priority Queue: The order of dequeuing is determined by the priority of the
elements, not their order of arrival.
c. Two types of priority queue:
a. Ascending priority queue (APQ)
b. Descending priority queue (DPQ)
APQ:
It is a collection of items into which items can be inserted arbitrarily and from which
only the smallest item can be removed.
Page 3 of 17
--- page 4 ---
If apq is an ascending priority queue, the operation pqinsert(apq,x) inserts element x
into apq
pqmindelete(apq) is the operation which will remove the minimum element from apq
and returns its value.
Once pqmindelete has been applied to retrieve the smallest element of an ascending
priority queue, it can be applied again to retrieve the next smallest, and so on.
Thus the operation successively retrieves elements of a priority queue in ascending
order.
DPQ:
It is a collection of items into which items can be inserted arbitrarily and from which
only the largest item can be removed.
If dpq is an descending priority queue, the operation pqinsert(dpq,x) inserts element x
into dpq
pqmaxdelete(dpq) is the operation which will remove the largest element from dpq and
returns its value.
Once pqmaxdelete has been applied to retrieve the largest element of an descending
priority queue, it can be applied again to retrieve the next largest, and so on.
Thus the operation successively retrieves elements of a priority queue in descending
order.
